content.title: How to Watch the Northern Lights Tonight Following Surge of Geomagnetic Storms Over the Weekend
content.text: NEED TO KNOW The northern lights may still be visible tonight through early March 24, after a weekend of strong geomagnetic stormsForecasters say auroras will likely appear in higher-latitude regions like northern U.S. states and Canada overnightDark, clear locations with an unobstructed northern view offer the best chance to see the auroras vividly If you missed the dazzling auroras over the weekend, you’re in luck because the skyshow isn’t over just yet! After powerful geomagnetic storms lit up skies across parts of the United States, the aurora borealis could still make an appearance tonight, March 23, into early Tuesday, March 24. ​​The northern lights (aurora borealis) are a result of geomagnetic storms, which occur when charged particles from the sun collide with gases in the Earth's atmosphere, creating brilliant waves of light in the sky. Still, their visibility depends on several factors, including intensity and location. According to forecasters at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), strong G3-level geomagnetic activity over the weekend pushed auroras unusually far south, creating vivid displays well beyond the usual polar regions. While tonight’s conditions are expected to be less intense, Earth’s magnetic field is still unsettled from recent solar activity, keeping the possibility of aurora sightings alive. Space weather experts say heightened solar winds and lingering storm effects could keep conditions active through the next couple of days, which means skywatchers still have a chance to catch the lights. Here’s everything you need to know about when, where and how to watch this stellar event. When will the northern lights be visible? Aurora borealis in Germany. RALF HIRSCHBERGER/AFP via Getty Look up tonight, because auroras are most likely to appear late this evening through the early morning hours of March 24, when skies are darkest. Still, geomagnetic activity is expected to remain somewhat elevated following the weekend's storms, increasing the chances of visible auroras overnight. Forecasters say active space weather conditions could continue through March 24 and 25 as the solar wind remains enhanced. Another solar eruption observed on March 22, however, could influence Earth's magnetic field later this week, potentially boosting geomagnetic activity. Where will the northern lights be visible? Northern Lights. Getty Tonight's auroras will likely be concentrated across higher-latitude regions, particularly in northern parts of the United States and Canada. Unlike the weekend, when strong storms pushed the light deep into mid-latitudes, tonight's displays are expected to stay closer to the northern horizon. Viewers in darker locations with clear weather and an unobstructed view of the northern horizon will have the best chance of spotting the phenomenon. How to watch the northern lights? Aurora borealis. SERGEI GAPON/AFP via Getty Find a dark location away from city lights, ideally with a clear view of the northern sky. The darker your surroundings, the more vivid the aurora colors will appear. Remember to also keep tabs on real-time conditions using NOAA’s 30-minute aurora forecast and space-weather apps that track solar wind and magnetic field changes. How to photograph the northern lights? You don’t need professional gear to capture the auroras... but it certainly helps! If you're hoping to photograph the northern lights, you'll want to keep your setup as steady as possible, since the auroras are best captured with long exposures. But if you have a smartphone handy, that works just fine. All you have to do is head to your device's settings and tap the "Night Mode" option or “Pro Mode” with similar exposure times.
